records.source: Πρὸ δὲ τῆς ἑορτῆς τοῦ πάσχα εἰδὼς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἦλθεν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὥρα ἵνα μεταβῇ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἀγαπήσας τοὺς ἰδίους τοὺς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς.
records.gloss: Before now the feast of the Passover, knowing the Jesus that came his the hour that he should pass out of the world this to the Father, having loved the own the [ones] in the world, to [the] end he loved them.

L.1: Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hour had come that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} should pass out of this world to the Father, having loved {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own who [were] in the world, loved them to the end.

R.1: It was just before the Passover festival. Jesus knew that {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hour had come, the time for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to leave this world and go to the Father. He had always loved the people in the world who belonged to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and now {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} loved them to the very end, with a love that held nothing back.

decisions.choice: to the end: both to the end of his life and to the uttermost, completely
alternatives: to the end (of his life) only
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean "to the end" in time or "completely, to the limit". Here both fit, and John seems to mean both: Jesus loved his own up to the end of his life, and he loved them with a love that went all the way. The noun is related to the verb Jesus speaks from the cross, "It is finished" (19:30). A footnote gives the second sense.

decisions.choice: his hour: the appointed time of his death and return to the Father, now come
decisions.reason: Until now the hour "had not yet come" (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). In 12:23 Jesus says that it has come. The narrator now says so too, and adds what the hour is: the time for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father, through his death.

decisions.choice: pass out of this world to the Father: Jesus's death seen as a going from one place to another
decisions.reason: The verb means to move or pass from one place to another, as in 5:24 ("has passed from death to life"). Jesus's death is his return to the Father from whom he came (16:28). "This world" here is the world in which people live, which Jesus is leaving and in which his own remain (17:11).

decisions.choice: his own: those who belong to Jesus, his disciples
decisions.reason: In 1:11 "his own" were his own people, who did not receive him. Here "his own" are those who did: the sheep who know his voice (10:3-4, 14), the people the Father has given him (17:6). They are "in the world" and will stay there when he goes (17:11). The love he had shown them all along now reaches its fullest point.

decisions.choice: before the Passover: the supper takes place on the evening before the feast
decisions.reason: In John the Jewish leaders have not yet eaten the Passover meal when Jesus is handed to Pilate (18:28), and he is condemned on the day of preparation for the Passover (19:14). The meal in this chapter is therefore before the Passover. John does not call it a Passover meal, as the other Gospels do (Mark 14:12-16).

decisions.choice: hour, at every level
decisions.reason: As in 12:23-27, the word stays "hour" at every level so that the thread of Jesus's hour can be followed through the Gospel (meaning decision m2). Readable adds "the time for him" to explain it.

decisions.choice: three sentences (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek is one sentence held together by two participles ("knowing", "having loved"). Balanced and Readable state the time, then what Jesus knew, then his love, each in its own sentence.

decisions.choice: had always loved; to the very end, with a love that held nothing back
decisions.reason: Readable gives both senses of the phrase (meaning decision m1), and "always" shows that "having loved" looks back over his whole time with them.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Pronouns for Jesus take the deity_pronoun setting; "He" at the start of a sentence is capitalized either way.

records.heading: Jesus washes the disciples' feet

records.source: καὶ δείπνου γινομένου, τοῦ διαβόλου ἤδη βεβληκότος εἰς τὴν καρδίαν ἵνα παραδοῖ αὐτὸν Ἰούδας Σίμωνος Ἰσκαριώτου, εἰδὼς ὅτι πάντα ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ὁ πατὴρ εἰς τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθεν καὶ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ὑπάγει, ἐγείρεται ἐκ τοῦ δείπνου καὶ τίθησιν τὰ ἱμάτια καὶ λαβὼν λέντιον διέζωσεν ἑαυτόν·
records.gloss: And supper taking place, the devil already having put into the heart that should betray him Judas [son] of Simon Iscariot, \v 3 knowing that all things gave to him the Father into the hands, and that from God he came out and to the God he is going away, \v 4 he rises from the supper and lays the garments, and having taken a towel he girded himself;

L.2: And while supper was taking place, the devil having already put into the heart that Judas [son] of Simon Iscariot should hand {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over,
L.3: [Jesus], knowing that the Father had given all things into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands, and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had come out from God and was going away to God,
L.4: rises from the supper and lays aside the garments, and taking a towel, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} tied [it] around {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

R.2: Jesus and the disciples were eating the evening meal. Even before this, the devil had put into the heart of Judas the idea of betraying Jesus. Judas was the son of Simon Iscariot.
R.3: Jesus knew that the Father had given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} power over everything. He also knew that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came from God and would soon go back to God.
R.4: He got up from the meal and took off {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} outer clothes. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} took a towel and tied it around {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} waist.

decisions.choice: while supper was taking place (SBLGNT)
alternatives: after supper, or when supper had begun (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Codex Vaticanus, the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some other early manuscripts have the present tense, "while supper was taking place". Many other manuscripts, followed by the KJV ("supper being ended"), have the aorist, which can mean "when supper was over". The washing happens during the meal, since Jesus gets up from it and returns to it (13:12) and the meal goes on afterward (13:26). A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the devil had put into the heart of Judas the purpose of betraying Jesus
alternatives: the devil had already decided in his own heart that Judas would betray him
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "put into the heart", without saying whose heart, and then names Judas as the one who would betray. The most natural reading is that the devil put the thought into Judas's heart; 13:27 says that Satan entered him. Many later manuscripts make this explicit by putting Judas's name in the form "of Judas", joined to "the heart". The words could also mean that the devil had made up his own mind that Judas would betray Jesus, since "to put into the heart" can mean "to decide". A footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: the devil: the enemy of God, already at work behind the betrayal
decisions.reason: John has called the devil a murderer and a liar (8:44) and called Judas "a devil" for doing his work (6:70). The word "already" shows that the betrayal is under way before Jesus begins to wash feet. Jesus serves even the one who will hand him over.

decisions.choice: hand him over: betray him; Judas son of Simon Iscariot, as in 6:71
decisions.reason: The verb means to hand over, and for Judas it means betrayal (6:64, 71). As in 6:71, the name Iscariot agrees in form with Simon, so it describes the father as well as the son.

decisions.choice: given all things into his hands: given him full authority over everything
decisions.reason: To give something into someone's hands is to put it under their power. John has said the same in 3:35 ("The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand"). Jesus goes to his death knowing that nothing is outside his control (10:18).

decisions.choice: knowing who he is, he rises to do a slave's task
decisions.reason: The long sentence sets Jesus's full knowledge of his authority, his origin and his goal right beside the plain actions that follow. He does not wash feet in spite of knowing who he is, nor because he forgets it; he does it knowing it. The same pattern of the Lord serving is drawn out in 13:13-16.

decisions.choice: the garments: his outer clothing, the cloak worn over the tunic
decisions.reason: The plural word means outer clothing, as in 19:23, where it is distinguished from the tunic. Jesus is left in the tunic, dressed like a slave for work.

decisions.choice: lays aside ... taking: perhaps an echo of laying down and taking up his life
alternatives: ordinary words for undressing and dressing, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: The verb "lays aside" is the one Jesus uses for laying down his life (10:11, 15, 17-18), and in 13:12 he "took" his garments again, the verb used for taking his life up again (10:17-18). The washing may picture his death. John does not say so, and both verbs are common, so this is uncertain.

decisions.choice: Historic present: rises, lays aside (L); got up, laid aside (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid ("he rises", "he lays aside", "he pours", "he comes", "he says"). Literal keeps the present throughout this passage so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, which is the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision applies to every historic present in 13:1-11.

decisions.choice: several sentences; laid aside (L), put aside (B), took off (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek is one long sentence: a setting, two things Jesus knew, then four actions. Balanced and Readable give each part its own sentence and name Jesus again so that the subject is clear.

decisions.choice: hand over (L); betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:64 and 6:71 (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: [Jesus] (L); the thought of, the heart of Judas (B); Jesus and the disciples were eating; the idea of (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek does not name Jesus as the subject of verses 3-4, since he was named in verse 1, so Literal supplies him in brackets. Balanced and Readable follow the reading in meaning decision m2 and say whose heart it was. Readable says who was eating.

decisions.choice: had given him power over everything
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom "into his hands" (meaning decision m5).

records.source: εἶτα βάλλει ὕδωρ εἰς τὸν νιπτῆρα, καὶ ἤρξατο νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας τῶν μαθητῶν καὶ ἐκμάσσειν τῷ λεντίῳ ᾧ ἦν διεζωσμένος.
records.gloss: Then he puts water into the basin, and began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe with the towel with which he was girded.

L.5: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} pours water into the basin, and began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe [them] with the towel which {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had tied on.

R.5: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} poured water into a large bowl. He began to wash the feet of the disciples and to dry them with the towel around {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} waist.

decisions.choice: washing feet: a task for a slave or the lowest member of a household
decisions.reason: People walked dusty roads in sandals, so a host gave guests water to wash their feet (Genesis 18:4; Luke 7:44). The washing itself was usually done by a slave; Abigail offers to wash the feet of David's servants as the lowest of slaves (1 Samuel 25:41). A teacher washing his disciples' feet reverses the usual order (13:13-16).

decisions.choice: began to wash: the one with all authority (13:3) does the slave's work
decisions.reason: John places this act directly after saying that the Father had given all things into Jesus's hands. The contrast is the point: Jesus uses his authority to serve. "Began" also prepares for Peter's interruption in verse 6.

decisions.choice: wipe: perhaps an echo of Mary wiping Jesus's feet (12:3)
decisions.reason: The verb "to wipe" is the one used of Mary, who anointed Jesus's feet and wiped them with her hair (12:3; 11:2). What Mary did for Jesus, Jesus now does for his disciples. The link is likely but not certain, since the verb is the natural one for drying.

decisions.choice: basin (L, B); large bowl (R); wipe (L); dry (B, R)
decisions.reason: The basin is a washing bowl. Balanced and Readable say "dry", which is what wiping wet feet with a towel does. Literal keeps "wipe" to show the link with 12:3 (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: pours ... began (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps John's change from present to past (historic present; see 13:2-4, decision r-en-1).

records.source: ἔρχεται οὖν πρὸς Σίμωνα Πέτρον.
records.gloss: He comes then to Simon Peter.

R.6: Then Jesus came to Simon Peter.

decisions.choice: so he comes: the story moves on to Peter; John does not say whether Peter was first
alternatives: Peter came after some of the others
decisions.reason: The word "so" carries the story forward. John does not say how many disciples Jesus had washed before he came to Peter, and the text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, since the sentence is short and stands at the start of a new scene.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, σύ μου νίπτεις τοὺς πόδας;
records.gloss: He says to him, "Lord, you of me wash the feet?"

L.6: He says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} wash my feet?"

R.6: Peter said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} really going to wash my feet?"

decisions.choice: you ... my: the two pronouns side by side show how wrong it seems to Peter
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written out for emphasis and placed next to "my": you, my Lord, wash my feet? The present tense can mean "are you about to", since Jesus has come to Peter but has not yet begun.

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of a disciple to his master
decisions.reason: Peter is one of the Twelve and speaks to Jesus as his Lord (6:68). In 13:13 Jesus himself says that they rightly call him Teacher and Lord.

decisions.choice: Peter; are you going to (B); are you really going to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker and use "going to" for an act that is about to happen (meaning decision m1). Readable adds "really" to show Peter's surprise.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Pronouns for Jesus, including "you" when Peter speaks to him, take the deity_pronoun setting. "My" here is Peter's and takes none.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ὃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ σὺ οὐκ οἶδας ἄρτι, γνώσῃ δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "What I do you not know now, you will know but after these things."
pieces: you will come to know it

L.7: Jesus answered and said to him, "What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know after these things."

R.7: Jesus answered, "You do not understand what I am doing right now. Later you will."

decisions.choice: I ... you: both pronouns are emphatic, setting what Jesus does against what Peter can grasp
decisions.reason: The Greek writes out both "I" and "you". Jesus answers Peter's emphatic "you" (13:6): what I am doing is beyond what you, as yet, understand.

decisions.choice: know ... will know: Peter does not grasp it now, but will come to understand
decisions.reason: John uses two different verbs for knowing here; together they say that Peter lacks understanding now and will gain it.

decisions.choice: after these things: after Jesus's death and resurrection
alternatives: in a few moments, when Jesus explains it (13:12-17)
decisions.reason: John often says that the disciples understood only later what Jesus did and said, when he was raised and glorified (2:22; 12:16), and the Spirit would remind them (14:26). Jesus explains part of the act at once (13:12-17), but its full meaning comes after the cross.

decisions.choice: know ... come to know (B); understand (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the move from not knowing to coming to know; Readable says "understand", the plain sense of both verbs here (meaning decision m2).

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ Πέτρος· Οὐ μὴ νίψῃς μου τοὺς πόδας εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
records.gloss: Says to him Peter, "Not not you may wash of me the feet into the age."

L.8: Peter says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You will by no means wash my feet, ever!"

R.8: Peter said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "No! I will never let {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} wash my feet!"

decisions.choice: the strongest possible refusal: never, not ever
decisions.reason: Two negatives together make the strongest denial Greek has, and "to the age" adds "ever". Peter is not asking; he refuses outright.

decisions.choice: Peter refuses out of respect for his Lord
decisions.reason: To Peter it is unthinkable that his Lord should do a slave's task for him (meaning decision m1 of 13:6). His refusal comes from honor for Jesus, but it also resists what Jesus has chosen to do, as Peter will later resist Jesus's arrest (18:10-11).

decisions.choice: never going to ... not ever (B); No! I will never let you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced repeats the negative to carry the force of the Greek. Readable turns it into Peter's refusal to allow it, which is what the strong negative means in the mouth of the one being served.

records.source: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς αὐτῷ· Ἐὰν μὴ νίψω σε, οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετ’ ἐμοῦ.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus him, "If not I wash you, not you have part with me."

L.8: Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no part with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

R.8: Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you cannot belong to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: a share with me: a place among those who belong to Jesus and share in what is his
alternatives: a share in the task of serving others
decisions.reason: The word means a part or share, as in an inheritance (Luke 15:12) or a portion in the land (the Levites had "no part or inheritance", Deuteronomy 12:12). To have a share "with" Jesus is to belong to him and share his life and his place with the Father (14:3; 17:24). Without what Jesus is doing, Peter cannot be one of his own (13:1).

decisions.choice: wash you: the washing points beyond the feet to the cleansing Jesus gives
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say "your feet" but "you". The washing stands for what Jesus does for his own through his death, which Peter does not yet understand (13:7). Peter must receive it, not refuse it.

decisions.choice: part (L); can have no share (B); cannot belong to (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "share", the word for a portion that belongs to someone; "can" makes clear that the second half follows from the first. Readable says what having a share with Jesus means (meaning decision m1); this narrows a word with a wider sense.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of himself, so "me" takes the deity_pronoun setting.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ Σίμων Πέτρος· Κύριε, μὴ τοὺς πόδας μου μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τὴν κεφαλήν.
records.gloss: Says to him Simon Peter, "Lord, not the feet of me only but also the hands and the head."

L.9: Simon Peter says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, not my feet only, but also the hands and the head!"

R.9: Simon Peter said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Then, Lord, do not wash only my feet. Wash my hands and my head too!"

decisions.choice: "wash" is understood: not only my feet, but my hands and head too
decisions.reason: Peter leaves out the verb; it is plain from what Jesus has just said.

decisions.choice: Peter swings from refusal to excess, still not understanding
decisions.reason: If being washed means having a share with Jesus, Peter wants as much of it as he can have. His eagerness is real, but he still thinks of the washing as a matter of how much water, which Jesus corrects in verse 10.

decisions.choice: Lord: a disciple's address to Jesus, as in 13:6
decisions.reason: Peter again calls Jesus Lord, as a disciple speaking to his master (13:6, 13).

decisions.choice: Then (B, R); wash (R)
decisions.reason: "Then" shows that Peter is answering what Jesus has just said. Readable supplies the verb Peter leaves out (meaning decision m1).

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὁ λελουμένος οὐκ ἔχει χρείαν εἰ μὴ τοὺς πόδας νίψασθαι, ἀλλ’ ἔστιν καθαρὸς ὅλος· καὶ ὑμεῖς καθαροί ἐστε, ἀλλ’ οὐχὶ πάντες.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "The [one] having been bathed not has need except the feet to wash, but is clean wholly; and you clean are, but not all."

L.10: Jesus says to him, "The one who has bathed has no need except to wash the feet, but is clean all over; and you are clean, but not all [of you]."

R.10: Jesus answered, "A person who has taken a bath is clean all over. Only the feet need washing. You are clean too, but not all of you."

decisions.choice: except the feet (SBLGNT)
alternatives: The one who has bathed has no need to wash, but is clean all over (Codex Sinaiticus and some Latin witnesses)
decisions.reason: Codex Sinaiticus and some Latin witnesses lack "except the feet". Without the words, Jesus says: "The one who has bathed has no need to wash, but is clean all over." Then the bath itself is the cleansing Jesus gives, and the foot-washing is that bath. Most manuscripts, among them early papyri and Codex Vaticanus, have the words; some add "only". A footnote gives the shorter reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: bathed: washed the whole body; wash: wash a part of the body
decisions.reason: Jesus uses two different verbs. The first is for bathing the whole body; the second, used throughout this passage for the feet, is for washing a part. A guest who had bathed at home needed only to wash the dust from the feet on arrival.

decisions.choice: clean: made clean by Jesus and belonging to him; the bath is a cleansing that need not be repeated
alternatives: the foot-washing is a further, repeated cleansing from daily wrongs for those already clean
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the picture of the bath to speak of a cleansing the disciples have already received. In 15:3 he says that they are clean because of the word he has spoken to them. The foot-washing may stand for that same cleansing given through his death, or for a further cleansing that those already clean still need. The text does not settle which. A footnote gives the second view.

decisions.choice: you are clean: Jesus turns from Peter to all the disciples, with one exception
decisions.reason: "You" is now plural. "Not all" points to Judas, as the narrator explains in verse 11. Judas has had his feet washed with the rest, but he is not clean.

decisions.choice: bathed / taken a bath; wash
decisions.reason: Every level keeps two different English verbs for the two Greek verbs (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: clean all over first, then the feet
decisions.reason: Readable puts the main point first in short sentences: the bathed person is clean, and only the feet need washing.

records.source: ᾔδει γὰρ τὸν παραδιδόντα αὐτόν· διὰ τοῦτο εἶπεν ὅτι Οὐχὶ πάντες καθαροί ἐστε.
records.gloss: He knew for the [one] betraying him; because of this he said that, "Not all clean you are."

L.11: For {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} knew the one handing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over; because of this {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Not all of you are clean."

R.11: Jesus knew who was going to betray {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Not all of you are clean."

decisions.choice: for: the narrator explains Jesus's words to the reader
decisions.reason: John steps in to explain "not all" (13:10). He does not say that the disciples understood it; in 13:28-29 they still do not know what Judas is about to do.

decisions.choice: the one handing him over: the betrayer, whose betrayal is already under way
decisions.reason: The participle is present: the betrayal is already set in motion (13:2), though not yet done. It can also be taken as "the one who would hand him over"; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: Jesus knew: he was not taken by surprise
decisions.reason: John has said from early on that Jesus knew who would betray him (6:64, 70-71), and Jesus will say so again (13:18-19). He washes Judas's feet with full knowledge.

decisions.choice: handing him over (L); was going to betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 13:2 and 6:71 (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: Jesus; So
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus and joins the two sentences with "So" for the Greek "because of this".

records.source: Ὅτε οὖν ἔνιψεν τοὺς πόδας αὐτῶν καὶ ἔλαβεν τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνέπεσεν, πάλιν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Γινώσκετε τί πεποίηκα ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: When therefore he washed the feet of them and took the garments of him and reclined, again he said to them, "Do you know what I have done to you?

L.12: So when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had washed their feet and taken {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} garments and reclined, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them again, "Do you know what I have done to you?

R.12: After Jesus had washed their feet, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} outer clothes back on and went back to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} place at the table. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spoke to them again. "Do you understand what I have done for you?

decisions.choice: again goes with "said": he spoke to them again (SBLGNT punctuation)
alternatives: again goes with "reclined": he reclined again, then said
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT puts its comma before "again", so the word begins the next clause: having taken his place, Jesus spoke to them again, after the exchange with Peter (13:6-11). Other editions put the comma after it, giving "reclined again". The sense hardly changes: he had got up from the meal (13:4), so taking his place at the table is a return either way.

decisions.choice: a question: Do you know what I have done to you?
alternatives: a command: Understand what I have done to you
decisions.reason: The verb form is the same for "you know" and "know!", so the words could be a question or a command. The SBLGNT prints a question, and Jesus goes on to explain the act himself (13:13-17), as a teacher does after asking his pupils. Either way he takes up what he said to Peter: "what I am doing you do not know now, but you will understand afterward" (13:7). The footnote gives the command.

decisions.choice: took his garments and reclined: he dressed again and returned to his place at the meal
decisions.reason: He had laid aside his outer garments to wash their feet (13:4). At a formal meal guests reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, so "reclined" means he took his place at the table again. The same pair of verbs, laying down and taking up, is used of his life in 10:17-18; John may intend the echo, so that the washing pictures his death and return, but he does not say so.

decisions.choice: Jesus (subject); outer clothes back on; took his place at the table (B), went back to his place at the table (R)
alternatives: he had washed; taken his garments; reclined (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus, since the last speaker in the scene was Peter (13:9). "Outer clothes" says what the garments were (meaning decision m3), and "took his place at the table" says what reclining at a meal meant.

decisions.choice: Do you understand ... for you (B, R)
decisions.reason: The question is about grasping the meaning of the act, which "understand" says. The washing was done to them and for their good, so Balanced and Readable say "for you"; Literal keeps "to you".

records.heading: An example to follow

records.source: ὑμεῖς φωνεῖτέ με Ὁ διδάσκαλος καὶ Ὁ κύριος, καὶ καλῶς λέγετε, εἰμὶ γάρ.
records.gloss: You call me 'the Teacher' and 'the Lord', and well you say, I am for.

L.13: You call {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} 'the Teacher' and 'the Lord,' and you say [it] well, for I am [so].

R.13: You call {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} your Teacher and your Lord. And you are right, because that is who I am.

decisions.choice: the Teacher and the Lord: titles, as the disciples addressed him
alternatives: the teacher and the lord as plain descriptions
decisions.reason: The two nouns stand in the naming case with the article, the way a title or a form of address is quoted. "Teacher" is John's own translation of "Rabbi" (1:38; 20:16), the name the disciples use for him (1:49; 4:31; 11:8). Jesus is repeating the titles they actually use.

decisions.choice: Lord: the disciples' title of respect for their master and teacher, which in John comes to mean more
decisions.reason: A disciple called his teacher "lord" as a mark of respect and of belonging to him, and the disciples use it throughout (6:68; 11:12; 13:6, 9). Jesus accepts the title. In John its meaning grows until Thomas says "My Lord and my God" (20:28). Here it sets up the argument of 13:14 and the saying about master and slave in 13:16, where the same word means a slave's owner.

decisions.choice: for I am: for I am the Teacher and the Lord; the predicate comes from the sentence
decisions.reason: "I am" here simply agrees with what they say: the titles they have just used are its complement. It is not the bare, unexplained "I am" of 13:19, where nothing in the sentence completes it.

decisions.choice: Teacher and Lord, capitalised; in quotation marks (L, B)
decisions.reason: They are titles for Jesus, so they are capitalised at every level, and "Lord" follows the book-wide choice for his disciples' address. Literal keeps the article ("the Teacher"); Readable says "your Teacher and your Lord" to make the titles plain without quotation marks.

decisions.choice: you say [it] well, for I am [so] (L); you are right, because that is what I am (B, R)
decisions.reason: A bare "for I am" would look like the absolute "I am" of 13:19; every level supplies the complement (meaning decision m3), Literal in brackets.

records.source: εἰ οὖν ἐγὼ ἔνιψα ὑμῶν τοὺς πόδας ὁ κύριος καὶ ὁ διδάσκαλος, καὶ ὑμεῖς ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας·
records.gloss: If therefore I washed of you the feet, the Lord and the Teacher, also you ought of one another to wash the feet;

L.14: If then I, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.

R.14: I am your Lord and your Teacher, and I have washed your feet. So you also should wash each other's feet.

decisions.choice: an argument from the greater to the lesser: since I, the Lord, did this, you can hardly refuse
decisions.reason: "If" here states a fact: he has washed their feet. Jesus now puts "Lord" before "Teacher", reversing the order of 13:13, which stresses his rank. If the one with the highest place did the lowest task, none of them can think it beneath him. The point returns as a saying in 13:16.

decisions.choice: washing feet: a slave's task, done for guests
decisions.reason: Roads were dusty and people wore sandals, so a host's slave washed the feet of guests (compare 1 Samuel 25:41, where Abigail offers to wash the feet of David's servants). A free man would not normally do it for his equals, still less a teacher for his disciples; this is why Peter objects (13:6-8).

decisions.choice: ought to wash one another's feet: the disciples are to serve one another as he served them, in the humblest tasks; whether the washing itself is also meant as a practice is left open
alternatives: a command to repeat the washing of feet as a regular practice
only a picture of humble service, not meant literally
decisions.reason: "Ought" is the language of a debt: what he has done puts them under an obligation to one another. Verse 15 calls the washing an example, and in 13:34 and 15:12 the command is to love one another as he loved them, which points beyond the act itself. But the early church did wash the feet of fellow believers: 1 Timothy 5:10 lists "washed the feet of the saints" among a widow's good works. The text supports at least humble service of one another; how far it also asks for the literal act is a judgment.

decisions.choice: have a duty to (B), should (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to owe, and so to be bound to do something. Balanced says "have a duty to" to keep the sense of a debt; Readable uses the plain "should". Readable turns the condition into two statements of fact, since the "if" assumes the washing happened (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ὑπόδειγμα γὰρ ἔδωκα ὑμῖν ἵνα καθὼς ἐγὼ ἐποίησα ὑμῖν καὶ ὑμεῖς ποιῆτε.
records.gloss: An example for I gave you, that just as I did to you also you may do.

L.15: For I gave you an example, so that just as I did to you, you also may do.

R.15: I have given you an example to follow. You should do for each other what I have done for you.

decisions.choice: example: a pattern given to be copied
alternatives: a mere illustration or object lesson
decisions.reason: The word means a pattern or model that others are meant to follow (James 5:10 uses it of the prophets as an example of patient suffering). The purpose clause that follows says the same: "so that you also may do".

decisions.choice: just as I did to you: the same kind of service, given in the same love
decisions.reason: "Just as" asks for more than copying the outward act: it asks them to serve as he served. John opens the scene with Jesus loving his own to the end (13:1), and the command of 13:34 has the same shape: "just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another". So the example reaches to the self-giving that the washing pictures (meaning decision m3 at 13:14).

decisions.choice: for: the example explains the duty of 13:14; "example" stands first for emphasis
decisions.reason: "For" gives the reason they owe one another this service: he did it as an example. The word stands first in the sentence, so the stress falls on it: what he did was meant to be followed.

decisions.choice: What I gave you was an example (B); an example to follow ... for each other (R)
alternatives: For I have given you an example (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the weight on "example" by putting it at the end of its clause (meaning decision m3). Readable adds "to follow" and "for each other", which come from the purpose clause and from 13:14.

records.source: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ ἔστιν δοῦλος μείζων τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ οὐδὲ ἀπόστολος μείζων τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you, not is a slave greater than the master of him, nor a sent one greater than the [one] having sent him.

L.16: Truly, truly I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor [is] a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

R.16: I tell you the truth: a servant is not more important than his master. And a messenger is not more important than the person who sent him.

decisions.choice: slave: a person owned by a master, with no rights of his own
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for a slave, someone who was another's property (8:34-35). In the household picture of this saying the slave owes everything to the master and has no standing above him. Jesus has just done a slave's task (13:14); his disciples are in the slave's place and cannot claim to be above it.

decisions.choice: his master: an ordinary owner in the saying, but the word is the one the disciples use for Jesus
decisions.reason: In the saying the master is simply a slave's owner. The word is the same as "Lord" in 13:13-14, so the hearers apply it at once: if their Lord has washed feet, his slaves cannot refuse to. Jesus repeats the saying in 15:20 to warn them that they will share his treatment; Matthew 10:24 has a similar saying.

decisions.choice: messenger: one sent on another's behalf, an envoy
alternatives: apostle, as the title of the Twelve
decisions.reason: This is the only time the noun occurs in John. It comes from the verb "to send" and here means anyone sent with a task, as the parallel "the one who sent him" shows; it is not yet the title of an office. An envoy acted with his sender's authority but was never above him (compare 12:44-45 and 13:20). The disciples are about to be sent (17:18; 20:21).

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 13:20 as well.

decisions.choice: slave (L), servant (B, R); master; messenger (L, R), one who is sent (B)
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable and "slave" in Literal, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that the slave was owned. "Master" is used because in the saying the word means an owner of slaves, not the title of 13:13 (meaning decision m2). "Apostle" would suggest the later office (meaning decision m3); Balanced says "one who is sent" so that the link with "the one who sent him" stays visible. "His" refers to the figure in the saying, so it takes no setting.

records.source: εἰ ταῦτα οἴδατε, μακάριοί ἐστε ἐὰν ποιῆτε αὐτά.
records.gloss: If these things you know, blessed are you if you do them.

L.17: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

R.17: Now you know these things. If you do them, God's blessing is on you.

decisions.choice: two different conditions: since you know (a fact), if you do (still open)
decisions.reason: The first "if" assumes what it states: they now know, because he has shown and explained it. The second "if" leaves the matter open: whether they will do it remains to be seen. Knowing is not yet blessing; doing is what counts (compare James 1:25).

decisions.choice: blessed: in a good state in God's sight, favored by him
alternatives: happy, in the sense of a feeling
decisions.reason: The word is the one used in the beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11) and in the Psalms (Psalm 1:1 in Greek). It declares a person well off before God, whatever they feel. It occurs twice in John, here and in 20:29 ("blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed").

decisions.choice: Now you know (B, R); act on them (B); God's blessing is on you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express the first condition as the fact it assumes (meaning decision m1). Balanced says "act on them" for doing what one has learned. "Blessed" is kept at Literal and Balanced; Readable names God as the one who blesses, which the word implies (meaning decision m2).

records.source: οὐ περὶ πάντων ὑμῶν λέγω· ἐγὼ οἶδα τίνας ἐξελεξάμην· ἀλλ’ ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ· Ὁ τρώγων μου τὸν ἄρτον ἐπῆρεν ἐπ’ ἐμὲ τὴν πτέρναν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Not about all of you I speak; I know whom I chose; but that the scripture may be fulfilled, 'The [one] eating of me the bread lifted up against me the heel of him.'

L.18: I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I chose. But [this is] so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: 'The one who eats {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} bread has lifted up his heel against {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.'

R.18: I am not talking about all of you. I know the ones I have chosen. But what the Scripture says must come true: 'The one who shares {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} bread has turned against {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.'

decisions.choice: I know whom I chose: he chose all twelve, Judas among them, and was not deceived about any of them
alternatives: he knows which of them are truly his chosen ones, and Judas is not among them (15:16)
decisions.reason: Jesus has just said that not all of them are clean (13:10-11). In 6:70 he says "Did I not choose you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil", and 6:64 says he knew from the beginning who would betray him. So the point is most likely that the betrayal will not take him by surprise. In 15:16 "I chose you" is said to the disciples who remain after Judas has gone, which allows the other reading.

decisions.choice: but so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: words are left out; the sense is "but this is happening so that"
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "but so that the Scripture may be fulfilled", with no main verb. The missing words are understood from the context: the choosing of a betrayer and what he is about to do happen so that Scripture is fulfilled. John uses the same short form in 9:3 and 15:25. "The Scripture" here means one particular passage.

decisions.choice: Psalm 41:10, quoted freely
decisions.reason: In the psalm the speaker, a righteous sufferer traditionally identified as David, laments that even his close friend, who ate his bread, has turned against him. John's wording is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek translation of the Psalms and leaves out the words about the friend "in whom I trusted". To eat a man's bread was to share his table and his friendship, so the betrayal comes from the closest circle (13:26). Reviewers should check the wording against the Greek and Hebrew of the psalm.

decisions.choice: lifted up his heel against me: has turned against me with contempt, as a betrayer
alternatives: tripping someone up, as a wrestler does
decisions.reason: The exact picture is uncertain: raising the heel may be the movement of a kick, of showing someone the sole of the foot as an insult, or of tripping an opponent. All of them express hostility and contempt from someone who should have been loyal. The past tense comes from the psalm; for Jesus the act is about to happen.

decisions.choice: eats: the verb John uses in 6:54-58, possibly an echo
alternatives: an ordinary word for eating, with no echo
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for eating the flesh of the Son of Man (6:54-58) and here; elsewhere in the New Testament it occurs only in Matthew 24:38. The echo would sharpen the irony: one who shared the table of the one who gives himself as bread turns against him. But the verb was also an everyday word for eating, so the link is possible, not certain.

decisions.choice: raised his heel against me (B); shares my bread, has turned against me (R)
alternatives: has lifted up his heel against me (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture, as the psalm does. Readable gives the sense of the idiom (meaning decision m4), and says "shares my bread" because eating someone's bread meant sharing their table (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: [this is] so that (L); it is happening so that (B); what the Scripture says must come true (R)
alternatives: but so that the Scripture may be fulfilled (no words supplied)
decisions.reason: English needs a main verb here (meaning decision m2): Literal supplies it in brackets, Balanced says "it is happening", and Readable gives the sense of necessity that the purpose clause carries.

records.source: ἀπ’ ἄρτι λέγω ὑμῖν πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι, ἵνα πιστεύσητε ὅταν γένηται ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι.
records.gloss: From now I tell you before the happening, so that you may believe when it happens that I am.

L.19: From now on I am telling you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am.

R.19: From now on I am telling you things before they happen. Then, when they happen, you will believe that I am.

decisions.choice: from now on: from this point Jesus tells them in advance what is coming
alternatives: now, at this moment, without the sense of continuing
decisions.reason: The phrase most often means "from now on" (14:7; Matthew 26:29, 64). It fits here: starting with the betrayal, Jesus now foretells what will happen, the betrayal (13:21), Peter's denial (13:38) and his own going away (14:29; 16:4), and 14:29 repeats the purpose: "I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe". The phrase can also mean simply "now"; the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: that I am: the words God uses of himself, said by Jesus of himself, as in 8:24 and 8:28
alternatives: a plain "that I am he": that I am the one I claim to be, the one Scripture speaks of
decisions.reason: As in 8:24 and 8:28, "I am" stands with nothing after it, and nothing in the sentence supplies a predicate; the nearest is "the one" of the psalm in 13:18, which is the betrayer, not Jesus. See meaning decision m1 at 8:24. The context here strengthens the echo of God's name (meaning decision m3). Some take it plainly as "I am he", the one I say I am; that reading is given in the footnote. Marked uncertain as at 8:24.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 43:10, and Isaiah's theme of the God who announces events before they happen
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 43:10 God says his servants are his witnesses "so that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (in Greek, "that I am"). The surrounding chapters prove the LORD's claim to be God by his telling of things before they happen (Isaiah 41:22-26; 43:9; 46:9-10; 48:3-5). Jesus does the same: he foretells his betrayal so that, when it comes, his disciples will believe. The betrayal, which might shake their trust, becomes evidence for it.

decisions.choice: that I am, with no "he" supplied
alternatives: that I am who I claim to be
decisions.reason: As at 8:24 and 8:28 (rendering decision r-en-1 at 8:24), every level keeps the bare words, because the echo of God's name is uppermost (meaning decision m2). The footnote gives "that I am he".

decisions.choice: things before they happen ... when they happen
decisions.reason: Readable makes "it" plural to say that from now on he foretells more than one event (meaning decision m1); the betrayal comes first.

records.source: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ λαμβάνων ἄν τινα πέμψω ἐμὲ λαμβάνει, ὁ δὲ ἐμὲ λαμβάνων λαμβάνει τὸν πέμψαντά με.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you, the [one] receiving whomever I send me receives, the [one] and me receiving receives the [one] having sent me."

L.20: Truly, truly I say to you, the one who receives whomever I send receives {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and the one who receives {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} receives the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

R.20: I tell you the truth: when people welcome anyone I send, they are welcoming {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. And when they welcome {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, they are welcoming the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: the envoy stands for the one who sends him: to receive the envoy is to receive the sender
decisions.reason: In Jewish practice, as across the ancient world, an envoy represented the one who sent him, so that the way he was treated was the way his sender was treated (12:44-45; Matthew 10:40; Luke 10:16). Jesus is the Father's envoy, and his disciples will be his (17:18; 20:21).

decisions.choice: receive: welcome and accept, both as a guest and as one whose message is believed
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in 1:12 ("as many as received him") and 5:43 ("you do not receive me"). It includes taking someone in as a guest, as travelling messengers depended on hospitality, and accepting the one who sent them.

decisions.choice: the saying takes up 13:16: the one sent is not above his sender, yet carries his authority
alternatives: a separate saying with no link to its context
decisions.reason: After the warning about the betrayer (13:18-19), Jesus returns to the picture of 13:16. His disciples are not greater than he is, but those he sends come with his authority and the Father's. The betrayal of one of them does not cancel the mission of the rest.

decisions.choice: welcomes (B), welcome (R); anyone ... someone (B), people ... anyone (R)
decisions.reason: "Welcome" says in everyday English what receiving a messenger meant (meaning decision m2). "Anyone", "someone" and "people" keep the saying general without he or she, so no gender setting is needed. The "Truly, truly" here follows rendering decision r-en-1 at 13:16.

records.source: Ταῦτα εἰπὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐταράχθη τῷ πνεύματι καὶ ἐμαρτύρησεν καὶ εἶπεν· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι εἷς ἐξ ὑμῶν παραδώσει με.
records.gloss: These things having said, the Jesus was troubled in the spirit and testified and said, "Truly truly I say to you that one of you will hand over me."

L.21: Having said these things, Jesus was troubled in spirit, and testified and said, "Truly, truly I say to you, one of you will hand {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} over."

R.21: After Jesus said this, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was deeply troubled in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit. He told them plainly, "I tell you the truth: one of you will betray {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: troubled in spirit: shaken within his own human spirit
decisions.reason: "Spirit" here is Jesus's own inner self, as in 11:33, where the same words describe him at the tomb of Lazarus. The verb is used of Jesus facing his death (12:27) and of the disciples' hearts (14:1, 27). Here he is shaken by what one of his own friends is about to do.

decisions.choice: testified: a solemn, open declaration
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for bearing witness to the truth (1:7, 34; 3:11; 5:31-39). Joined to "said", it marks what follows as a formal statement made in front of them all: Jesus is not guessing, and he is not taken by surprise (13:18-19).

decisions.choice: one of you will hand me over: one of the Twelve will betray him
decisions.reason: As in 6:64, 6:71 and 12:4, the verb means to hand someone over, and used of Judas it means betrayal. "One of you" puts the betrayer inside the circle at the table, as Psalm 41:10, just quoted (13:18), had said: the one who eats his bread.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: testified and said (L); solemnly declared (B); told them plainly (R); hand over (L); betray (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say in one verb what "testified and said" means (meaning decision m2). As in 6:64, 6:71 and 12:4, Literal keeps the plain sense of "hand over", and Balanced and Readable say what Judas's handing over was (m3). Balanced uses "is going to" for the future, which here means what is about to happen.

records.heading: One of you will betray me

records.source: ἔβλεπον εἰς ἀλλήλους οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀπορούμενοι περὶ τίνος λέγει.
records.gloss: Were looking at one another the disciples, being at a loss about whom he speaks.

L.22: The disciples were looking at one another, at a loss about whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking.

R.22: The disciples looked at each other. They had no idea which one of them {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was talking about.

decisions.choice: at a loss: puzzled, not knowing what to make of it
decisions.reason: The verb describes being at a loss or perplexed, as the women were at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4) and Paul was about the Galatians (Galatians 4:20). The disciples do not suspect anyone in particular; each of the other Gospels says they asked, one after another, whether it was they (Mark 14:19; Matthew 26:22).

decisions.choice: were looking: the imperfect pictures them glancing from one to another
decisions.reason: The tense shows an action going on, as they looked around the table at each other. The next verses take place while they are still wondering.

decisions.choice: he speaks: the present tense of the question as they asked it
decisions.reason: Greek keeps the tense of the question in their minds ("about whom is he speaking?"). It is not a separate historic present, and it is told in the past along with the rest of the sentence.

decisions.choice: which of them (B); which one of them (R)
decisions.reason: "Whom" means one of the people at the table, since Jesus had said "one of you" (verse 21). Balanced and Readable make that plain.

records.source: ἦν ἀνακείμενος εἷς ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὃν ἠγάπα ὁ Ἰησοῦς·
records.gloss: Was reclining one of the disciples of him in the bosom of the Jesus, whom was loving the Jesus;

L.23: One of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples was reclining in the bosom of Jesus, [the one] whom Jesus loved.

R.23: One of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples was lying right next to Jesus at the table, close to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} chest. He was the disciple whom Jesus loved.

decisions.choice: reclining in the bosom: lying next to Jesus at the meal, with his head near Jesus's chest
alternatives: sitting on a chair beside him
decisions.reason: At a formal meal, and at Passover above all, guests lay on couches or cushions around a low table, leaning on the left elbow and eating with the right hand. The one who lay to someone's right had his head close to that person's chest, so he was said to be "in his bosom". It was a place of closeness at the table, and of honor. Verse 25 shows the position: he only has to lean back to speak to Jesus privately.

decisions.choice: whom Jesus loved: a disciple John does not name
decisions.reason: This is the first time the Gospel speaks of a disciple in this way; he appears again at the cross (19:26), at the empty tomb (20:2), and by the lake (21:7, 20). The Gospel never gives his name. The closing verses say that he is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote them (21:20-24). Christian tradition from the second century identifies him as John the son of Zebedee, whom this Gospel never names either; others have suggested Lazarus, whom Jesus is also said to love (11:3, 5). The text itself leaves him unnamed. Jesus's love for him does not mean he loved the others less (13:1, 34).

decisions.choice: in the bosom of Jesus: possibly an echo of the Son in the bosom of the Father
alternatives: a plain description of where he lay, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: The same expression describes the Son "in the bosom of the Father" in 1:18, the one who has made the Father known. Here the disciple is in the bosom of Jesus, and he will become the witness who makes Jesus known (21:24). John may intend the parallel; the words also have their everyday meaning at a meal (m1), so the echo cannot be proved.

decisions.choice: in the bosom of Jesus (L); close beside him (B); right next to Jesus ... close to his chest (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as 1:18, so the same English: Literal "in the bosom", Balanced "close beside". Readable says plainly where he lay at the table, as meaning decision m1 describes.

decisions.choice: [the one] whom Jesus loved (L); the disciple whom Jesus loved (B, R)
decisions.reason: Throughout John he is "the disciple whom Jesus loved", never named and never given a new title. Literal keeps the clause at the end, where the Greek has it; Balanced and Readable use the full phrase so that readers meet it here in the form it will keep.

records.source: νεύει οὖν τούτῳ Σίμων Πέτρος πυθέσθαι τίς ἂν εἴη περὶ οὗ λέγει.
records.gloss: Nods therefore to this one Simon Peter to inquire who it might be about whom he speaks.

L.24: So Simon Peter nods to this one to inquire who it might be of whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} speaks.

R.24: So Simon Peter made a sign to that disciple. He wanted him to find out from Jesus which one {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} meant.

decisions.choice: to inquire who it might be (SBLGNT)
alternatives: and says to him, "Tell us who it is"
decisions.reason: Some important manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus, have Peter speak: "and he says to him, 'Say who it is of whom he speaks.'" Others, together with the SBLGNT, have only the sign and its purpose; Codex Sinaiticus combines the two. The meaning is much the same: Peter wants the disciple next to Jesus to find out. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: nods: makes a sign with the head, without speaking
decisions.reason: The verb means to nod or beckon (Acts 24:10). Peter signals rather than asking aloud. He was probably not lying next to Jesus himself, and the question could not be asked openly across the table.

decisions.choice: to inquire who it might be: to find out, by asking Jesus
decisions.reason: The mood of "might be" makes the question tentative, as a question one is not sure can be answered. The next verse shows how the disciple found out: he asked Jesus directly.

decisions.choice: nods (Literal); signaled (Balanced); made a sign (Readable); likewise in verses 25, 26 and 27
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("he nods", "he says", "he answers", "he gives") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage (verses 24, 25, 26 and 27).

decisions.choice: that disciple ... He wanted him to find out from Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says who "this one" is and whom he was to ask, as verse 25 shows (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἀναπεσὼν ἐκεῖνος οὕτως ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λέγει αὐτῷ· Κύριε, τίς ἐστιν;
records.gloss: Having leaned back that one thus upon the chest of the Jesus says to him, "Lord, who is it?"

L.25: That one, leaning back thus on the chest of Jesus, says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, who is it?"

R.25: So that disciple leaned back against Jesus's chest and asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Lord, who is it?"

decisions.choice: leaning back thus: tipping his head back against Jesus's chest, from where he lay
decisions.reason: The verb means to lean or fall back. "Thus" means just as he was, without changing his place at the table (verse 23). Lying beside Jesus, he had only to lean back for his head to rest against Jesus's chest, where he could ask quietly. "Chest" is a different word from "bosom" in verse 23; it names the body itself.

decisions.choice: leaning back thus (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have a verb meaning "falling on" in place of "leaning back", and some important manuscripts leave out "thus". Neither change alters the scene. No footnote is needed. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Lord: the address of a disciple to his teacher and master
decisions.reason: The disciples call Jesus "Lord" (6:68; 11:12; 13:6, 9), and he has just accepted the title (13:13).

decisions.choice: as he lay ... the disciple asked (B); So that disciple leaned back ... and asked (R)
alternatives: That one, leaning back thus, says (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced gives "thus" as "as he lay" (meaning decision m1); both say who "that one" is. Both use the past tense (see verse 24, rendering decision r-en-1).

records.source: ἀποκρίνεται ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν ᾧ ἐγὼ βάψω τὸ ψωμίον καὶ δώσω αὐτῷ· βάψας οὖν τὸ ψωμίον δίδωσιν Ἰούδᾳ Σίμωνος Ἰσκαριώτου.
records.gloss: Answers the Jesus, "That one it is for whom I will dip the morsel and will give to him." Having dipped therefore the morsel he gives [it] to Judas of Simon Iscariot.

L.26: Jesus answers, "It is that one for whom I will dip the morsel and give [it] to him." So having dipped the morsel, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gives [it] to Judas [son] of Simon Iscariot.

R.26: Jesus answered, "I am going to dip this piece of bread and give it to one of you. He is the one." Then Jesus dipped the bread and gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.

decisions.choice: the morsel: a small piece of bread, dipped into the common dish
alternatives: the bread of the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: The word means a small bite or piece, normally of bread. At the meal the diners dipped bread into a shared bowl of sauce (Mark 14:20). John does not tell of Jesus giving thanks over the bread and the cup at this meal, and nothing here suggests that this piece of bread is part of such a rite.

decisions.choice: giving a dipped morsel: a gesture of friendship toward a guest
alternatives: only a sign to point out the betrayer
decisions.reason: A host might honor a guest by dipping a piece of bread and handing it to him. If that is so here, Jesus's last act toward Judas is one of friendship, which makes the betrayal darker and fulfills the scripture just quoted: the one who eats Jesus's bread has lifted his heel against him (13:18; Psalm 41:10). How widely the custom was practiced is not certain; the gesture is at least a sign of shared table fellowship.

decisions.choice: he gives (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Some important manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus, read "he takes and gives", in words that recall the accounts of the Lord's Supper. Others, among them an early papyrus and Codex Sinaiticus, have only "he gives", as the SBLGNT does. The sense is the same. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Iscariot, describing Simon: Judas son of Simon Iscariot (SBLGNT)
alternatives: Judas son of Simon, from Kerioth
decisions.reason: As in 6:71, the name Iscariot agrees in form with Simon, so it belongs to the father as well as the son. Many later manuscripts make it agree with Judas, and a few have "from Kerioth". A footnote gives the other readings. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: this piece of bread, the bread (B, R); I will dip ... he is the one (B, R)
alternatives: It is the one to whom I give (Literal order)
decisions.reason: "Piece of bread" says in common words what the morsel was (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps "morsel". Balanced and Readable tell the action first and then say "he is the one", which is the natural order for this answer in this language.

decisions.choice: [son] of Simon (L); son of Simon (B); the son of Simon (R)
decisions.reason: As in 6:71, the Greek gives the father's name without a noun, and "son" is understood.

records.source: καὶ μετὰ τὸ ψωμίον τότε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς.
records.gloss: And after the morsel then entered into that one the Satan.

L.27: And after the morsel, then Satan entered into that one.

R.27: As soon as Judas took the bread, Satan went into him.

decisions.choice: Satan: the enemy of God, the same figure as the devil in 13:2
alternatives: a figure of speech for Judas's own evil
decisions.reason: This is the only time John uses the name Satan, which means "adversary". In 13:2 the devil had already put the plan to betray Jesus into Judas's heart; now he takes hold of Judas himself. Luke says the same in almost the same words (Luke 22:3). John holds both together: Satan is at work, and Judas is responsible for what he does (6:70-71; 12:6).

decisions.choice: after the morsel, then: at that very point, not because of the bread
alternatives: the bread was the means by which Satan entered
decisions.reason: "Then" stresses the moment: once Judas had taken the bread Jesus offered, Satan entered him. The gift of friendship (verse 26) is followed by the decisive turn. John does not say that the bread caused it.

decisions.choice: entered into him: took control of him
decisions.reason: To "enter into" a person is said of evil spirits taking possession (Mark 5:12-13; Luke 8:30). Here it means that Judas now gave himself over completely to Satan's purpose.

decisions.choice: Once Judas had received the bread (B); As soon as Judas took the bread (R); him
alternatives: After the bread, then Satan entered into that one (Literal)
decisions.reason: "After the morsel" means after Judas had received it (verse 30). Balanced and Readable say so, and name Judas, since "that one" could be unclear. "Once" and "as soon as" give the force of "then" (meaning decision m2).

records.source: λέγει οὖν αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὃ ποιεῖς ποίησον τάχιον.
records.gloss: Says therefore to him the Jesus, "What you are doing, do more quickly."

L.27: So Jesus says to him, "What you are doing, do more quickly."

R.27: Jesus said to him, "Do what you are going to do, and do it fast."

decisions.choice: what you are doing: what Judas has already set in motion
alternatives: what you are in the habit of doing
decisions.reason: The present tense speaks of the plan as already under way. Judas had made up his mind (13:2), and Jesus shows that he knows.

decisions.choice: more quickly: quickly, at once
decisions.reason: The word is a comparative, "more quickly", but such forms are often used with the plain sense "quickly" or "without delay". Where John uses it of the race to the tomb (20:4), a real comparison is meant; here no one else is in view.

decisions.choice: Jesus remains in command of the events leading to his death
alternatives: Jesus approves of what Judas is doing
decisions.reason: Jesus does not approve the betrayal; he has just called it a fulfillment of scripture done by one who shares his bread (13:18). His words show that his death is not forced on him: he lays down his life of his own accord (10:18), and the hour has come (13:1).

decisions.choice: what you are going to do
decisions.reason: The plan was under way but the deed itself had not yet been done (meaning decision m1). Readable says plainly that it was about to happen.

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τῶν ἀνακειμένων πρὸς τί εἶπεν αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: This but no one knew of the [ones] reclining for what he said to him;

L.28: But no one of those reclining [at the table] knew for what [reason] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said this to him.

R.28: But nobody at the table understood why Jesus said this to Judas.

decisions.choice: those reclining: the people at the meal
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 23 describes the guests lying at the table (meaning decision m1 there).

decisions.choice: no one: the others did not understand the purpose of Jesus's words
alternatives: the disciple whom Jesus loved did not know who the betrayer was
decisions.reason: Jesus had answered the disciple whom Jesus loved by pointing to the one who would receive the bread (verse 26). John does not say whether that disciple saw what it meant at once, or passed it on to Peter. What none of them understood was why Jesus sent Judas away; the next verse gives their guesses.

decisions.choice: knew for what: understood for what purpose
decisions.reason: They had heard the words; they did not know their purpose. The phrase asks what the words were for.

decisions.choice: Jesus ... Judas
decisions.reason: Readable names both people, since "he" and "him" could be confused.

records.source: τινὲς γὰρ ἐδόκουν, ἐπεὶ τὸ γλωσσόκομον εἶχεν Ἰούδας, ὅτι λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀγόρασον ὧν χρείαν ἔχομεν εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν, ἢ τοῖς πτωχοῖς ἵνα τι δῷ.
records.gloss: Some for were thinking, since the money box had Judas, that says to him the Jesus, "Buy [the things] of which need we have for the feast," or to the poor that something he should give.

L.29: For some were thinking, since Judas had the money box, that Jesus was saying to him, "Buy what we have need of for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor.

R.29: Judas was in charge of the group's money box. So some of them thought Jesus was telling him to buy what they needed for the festival. Others thought Jesus wanted him to give some money to poor people.

decisions.choice: had the money box: kept the group's common money
alternatives: owned a box of his own
decisions.reason: As in 12:6, the money box is the box in which Jesus and his disciples kept their money, and Judas was in charge of it. That is why the others thought Jesus was sending him on an errand.

decisions.choice: the feast: the Passover festival, which was about to begin
decisions.reason: John set this meal "before the feast of the Passover" (13:1). The festival, with the Feast of Unleavened Bread joined to it, lasted seven days, and food and other things had to be bought for it. The disciples' guess fits a time when the feast was still ahead; compare 18:28, where the next morning the authorities had not yet eaten the Passover.

decisions.choice: give something to the poor: giving alms, a recognized duty
decisions.reason: Giving to the poor was a religious duty in Israel (Deuteronomy 15:11), and Passover was a time when the poor were remembered. The group seems to have done so from its common money (12:5-6).

decisions.choice: Jesus says to him: the words as the disciples imagined them
decisions.reason: The present tense gives what they supposed Jesus was saying, in the form they imagined it; then the sentence changes to reported speech for the second guess ("that he should give").

decisions.choice: money box (all levels)
decisions.reason: The same words as in 12:6, so that readers can see that it is the same box and the same Judas.

decisions.choice: the group's money box; Others thought; some money
decisions.reason: Readable splits the two guesses into separate sentences and says what Judas would have given. As in 12:6, it adds whose money box it was.

records.source: λαβὼν οὖν τὸ ψωμίον ἐκεῖνος ἐξῆλθεν εὐθύς.
records.gloss: Having received therefore the morsel that one went out immediately.

L.30: So having received the morsel, that one went out immediately.

R.30: Judas took the bread and left right away.

decisions.choice: having received ... went out immediately: Judas leaves as soon as he has the bread
alternatives: he ate it and then left
decisions.reason: The participle and "immediately" tie his leaving closely to receiving the bread and to Jesus's words, "Do quickly what you are doing" (verse 27).

decisions.choice: went out: left the room and the company of Jesus and the disciples
decisions.reason: He leaves the meal to carry out the betrayal. He will next appear in the garden, leading the soldiers and the officers (18:2-3).

decisions.choice: Judas (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Judas for "that one", so the reader does not take it to be the disciple last mentioned in verse 25.

records.source: ἦν δὲ νύξ.
records.gloss: Was and night.

decisions.choice: night: the time of day; the meal was held after dark
decisions.reason: The Passover meal was eaten at night (Exodus 12:8), and this meal, held at the same season, was also at night. Judas goes out into the dark.

decisions.choice: night: also the darkness that Jesus, the light, had spoken of
alternatives: only a note of the time
decisions.reason: John often sets light against darkness (1:5; 3:19; 8:12). Jesus had said that night comes when no one can work (9:4), that whoever walks in the night stumbles (11:10), and that those who walk in darkness do not know where they are going (12:35). The short sentence, placed where it is, seems to carry that weight as Judas leaves the light. John does not spell it out, and the plain sense stands first.

decisions.choice: And it was night (L, B); It was night (R)
decisions.reason: The sentence is three words in Greek, and its force lies in its shortness (meaning decision m2). Every level keeps it short and adds nothing; Readable drops only "And".

records.source: Ὅτε οὖν ἐξῆλθεν λέγει Ἰησοῦς· Νῦν ἐδοξάσθη ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, καὶ ὁ θεὸς ἐδοξάσθη ἐν αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: When therefore he went out, says Jesus, "Now was glorified the Son of the Man, and the God was glorified in him;

L.31: So when he had gone out, Jesus says, "Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.31: After Judas left, Jesus said, "The time has come. Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God's glory is shown in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: When he had gone out: Judas's leaving (13:30) opens what follows
decisions.reason: "Therefore" ties these words to 13:30: Judas has taken the piece of bread and gone out into the night to betray Jesus. With the betrayer gone, Jesus speaks to the eleven alone. Here his farewell words to the disciples begin; they run on to his prayer in chapter 17 (13:31-17:26).

decisions.choice: has been glorified: a past tense for what is about to happen
alternatives: glorified already in his past ministry and signs only
a simple statement about the present moment
decisions.reason: The hour of the Son of Man's glorifying is his death, resurrection and return to the Father (12:23, 27-28; 17:1, 5). Judas's going out has set it in motion, so Jesus speaks of it as already done: it is that certain, and it has begun. "Now" marks this moment as the turning point. Verse 32 then speaks of the same glorifying in the future.

decisions.choice: God has been glorified in him: God's glory is shown in the Son and in what he does
alternatives: God is glorified by him, as an instrument only
decisions.reason: "In him" means in the Son's person and in his obedient work, above all his death. Jesus says the same in prayer: he has glorified the Father by finishing the work given him (17:4). The Father's glory and the Son's are bound together (12:28; 14:13).

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also verses 36, 37 and 38
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("says", "answers") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies to every such verb in the passage ("says" in verses 36 and 37, "answers" in verse 38). "Answered" in verse 36 is already a past tense in Greek.

decisions.choice: Judas (B, R); The time has come, and God's glory is shown in him (R); has now been glorified ... in him God has been glorified (B)
alternatives: Now the Son of Man has been glorified (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the one who went out (13:30). Readable says plainly that the time has come and uses the present "is glorified", to show that the glorifying is happening now and is about to be completed (meaning decision m2); it says that God's glory "is shown" in the Son, which is what being glorified in him means (meaning decision m3). Balanced puts "in him" first to keep the stress on the Son.

records.heading: A new commandment

records.source: εἰ ὁ θεὸς ἐδοξάσθη ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ ὁ θεὸς δοξάσει αὐτὸν ἐν αὑτῷ, καὶ εὐθὺς δοξάσει αὐτόν.
records.gloss: If the God was glorified in him, also the God will glorify him in himself, and at once will glorify him.

L.32: If God has been glorified in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, God will also glorify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, and will glorify {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} at once.

R.32: Since God has been glorified in the Son, God will also glorify the Son with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own glory. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will do it very soon.

decisions.choice: If God has been glorified in him (SBLGNT, included)
alternatives: the clause is left out (P66, Sinaiticus first hand, Vaticanus, Bezae and others)
decisions.reason: Several of the oldest manuscripts lack these words, among them Papyrus 66, the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Bezae, with some others. Many manuscripts have them, among them Codex Alexandrinus and the corrector of Sinaiticus. A copyist's eye could easily jump from "in him" at the end of verse 31 to the same words here and leave the clause out; the clause could also have been added to link the two verses. The SBLGNT includes it, and the sense is not changed much either way. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: if: a condition taken as true (since)
alternatives: a real doubt whether God has been glorified
decisions.reason: The "if" picks up the statement Jesus has just made in verse 31; it reasons from it, not doubting it.

decisions.choice: in himself: in God himself, that is, in God's own glory
decisions.reason: The word for "himself" is the reflexive form in the SBLGNT, which normally points back to the subject of its clause, here God. The Son is then taken up into the Father's own glory, as Jesus prays in 17:5 to be glorified in the Father's presence with the glory he had with him before the world existed. The earliest manuscripts had no breathing marks, so the same letters could be read as "in him", meaning in the Son; then the Son's glory comes from within his own person. Both readings say that God will glorify the Son.

decisions.choice: at once: without delay, in the coming events
alternatives: at the end of the age
decisions.reason: The glorifying does not wait for a distant future. It comes within days, in the cross, the resurrection and his going to the Father (12:23; 17:1, 5).

decisions.choice: deity_pronoun on every pronoun, for God and for the Son
decisions.reason: Every pronoun in this verse refers to God or to the Son, so each one takes the setting, "himself" included, whichever of them it means (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: the Son; with his own glory; very soon
decisions.reason: Readable names the Son, so the reader can tell the two persons apart, and follows meaning decision m3 in saying "with his own glory" for "in himself". That is an interpretation, marked uncertain there. "Since" shows that the "if" is taken as true (meaning decision m2).

records.source: τεκνία, ἔτι μικρὸν μεθ’ ὑμῶν εἰμι· ζητήσετέ με, καὶ καθὼς εἶπον τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὅτι Ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν, καὶ ὑμῖν λέγω ἄρτι.
records.gloss: Little children, yet a little [while] with you I am; you will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, 'Where I go you not are able to come,' also to you I say now.

L.33: Little children, yet a little [while] I am with you. You will seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and just as I said to the Jews, 'Where I go, you cannot come,' I also say to you now.

R.33: My dear children, I will be with you just a little longer. You will look for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Earlier I told the Jews, 'You are not able to come where I am going.' Now I am telling you the same thing.

decisions.choice: Little children: a tender address, as of a teacher or father to his own
decisions.reason: The word is a small, affectionate form of "children" and appears only here in this Gospel. The writer of 1 John uses it often for his readers (1 John 2:1, 12, 28; 3:7, 18; 4:4; 5:21). The word already takes in men and women.

decisions.choice: yet a little while: the short time left before his death and going away
decisions.reason: Jesus said the same to the crowds and the authorities (7:33; 12:35); he will say it again to the disciples (14:19; 16:16-19). The time is now a matter of hours.

decisions.choice: the Jews: those who heard him say this before (7:33-34; 8:21)
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus points back to a particular occasion: the crowd and the authorities in the temple courts to whom he said these words (7:32-36; 8:21-22). The word John wrote is kept and tied to that occasion. Jesus and the disciples he is speaking to are Jews themselves.

decisions.choice: Where I go you cannot come: Jesus quotes his own words in 8:21 (and 7:34)
decisions.reason: The words are the same, but their meaning for the disciples differs. To his opponents Jesus added "you will die in your sin" (8:21). To the disciples he adds "now": they cannot come yet, but they will follow later (verse 36; 14:2-3).

decisions.choice: seek / search for / look for; Where I go, you cannot come (L); You cannot come where I am going (B); You are not able to come where I am going (R)
decisions.reason: The quotation keeps the English each level used in 8:21, and "seek" keeps the English of 7:34, so that readers can see that Jesus is repeating himself.

decisions.choice: My dear children; Earlier I told
decisions.reason: Readable gives the tenderness of the address in everyday words and says plainly that Jesus is pointing back to an earlier time.

records.source: ἐντολὴν καινὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους.
records.gloss: A commandment new I give to you, that you love one another; just as I loved you, that also you love one another.
